title: The Anthropology of School Rituals
author: David Didau
summary: In the third of a series viewing schools through different disciplinary lenses, David Didau applies anthropology to argue that schools are best understood not as rational institutions devoted to teaching and learning but as cultures held together by ritual, symbol, and shared belief, in the Durkheimian sense that ceremonies matter less for what they claim to express than for the social solidarity they renew. Drawing on Harvey Whitehouse's distinction between frequent, unremarkable 'doctrinal' rituals (registration, corridor routines) and rare, emotionally intense 'imagistic' ones (prize-giving, leavers' assemblies), Didau argues schools depend on a mix of both to bind communities together and make daily life psychologically predictable, citing research showing rituals reduce anxiety even when they cannot plausibly affect outcomes. He extends Mary Douglas's account of symbolic boundary-making ('dirt' as matter out of place) to explain why seemingly trivial rules about uniform, movement, and classroom conduct actually police who belongs to a school's culture, and uses Victor Turner's concept of liminality to explain transition rituals like GCSE exam halls and leavers' assemblies. The essay's sharpest institutional critique borrows DiMaggio and Powell's 'mimetic isomorphism' and Meyer and Rowan's concept of 'decoupling' to explain how practices like purple-pen marking or scripted retrieval-practice starters spread system-wide not because they work, but because schools imitate what looks legitimate under uncertainty, stripping away the original problem-solving logic that gave the practice meaning in the first place.
points: Didau's central anthropological reframe, that schools are cultures held together by ritual and symbol rather than rational institutions optimized for learning, explains why practices that fail an efficiency test (assemblies, staff briefings) nonetheless persist.

The doctrinal/imagistic ritual distinction (frequent, unremarkable routines vs. rare, emotionally intense ceremonies) gives leaders a vocabulary for why students forget headteacher speeches but remember the events at which they were given.

The 'purple pen' and scripted retrieval-practice examples operationalize mimetic isomorphism and decoupling: practices spread across schools because they signal legitimacy to inspectors and peers, stripped of the specific reasoning that made them work in their original context.

Didau's use of Mary Douglas's 'dirt is matter out of place' explains why apparently trivial rules (blazers on chairs vs. floors, talking in class vs. exams) function as symbolic boundary markers that define in-group belonging, not as arbitrary discipline.

The GCSE exam hall and leavers' assembly are used as concrete examples of Victor Turner's liminality, moments deliberately ritualized to mark identity transitions ('candidate,' then 'leaver') that carry no direct academic function.
quotes: Rituals don't endure because they're the most efficient way of doing something but because they address deeper social issues that become part of the background of everyday life.
This is the third in a series of essays looking at schools through different disciplinary lenses. This week I'm going to explore what schools might look like through the eyes of an anthropologist.

Through repeated acts of gathering, singing, speaking and remembering, societies continually renew what Durkheim called social solidarity: the shared sense that individuals belong to a moral community larger than themselves.

Psychologists Michael Norton and Francesca Gino have shown that rituals reduce anxiety and increase our sense of control even when there's no plausible way they could influence outcomes. Their power lies in changing our relationship to uncertainty.

For instance, at some point in the last fifteen years, some school leader somewhere decided students should respond to feedback using purple pen. Whatever the rationalisation, the choice was almost certainly arbitrary.

Ideas are rarely copied in their entirety. We borrow what's easy to imitate, jettisoning the deeper beliefs, assumptions and purposes that originally gave a ritual meaning. That is one reason why edu-fads spread so quickly to so little effect.
Year 11s are no longer students, they become 'candidates' who are no longer ordinary members of the school community, but they haven't yet become school leavers.
